title: Why New Orleans produced few blues players
summary: Rose says whorehouse pianists played classical pieces, blues was not indigenous, and dances were the bulk of the repertoire.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: I know. I can restructure the whole area, right? Yeah. I'll tell you a joke, whether or not, but... Poor House is on Graffier Street. Yeah. And, and the, and the Supreme Court is right with it. Yeah. I think that's got this correct logic, I think, going on. Anyway, uh, I'm probably ahead of myself, yeah. Um, yeah, well, when he worked here in the saloons, were, were, were, I was saying that he played a lot of blues because there was, he was working for a prostitute audience, a lot of it, a lot of it.

Well, they didn't particularly go for the blues. Really? That wasn't their music. Uh-huh. You know, the, the test piece that they used for the piano players in the whorehouses, Yeah. was Poets and Peasant Overture. If you couldn't play that, you didn't get the job. Poets and Peasant Overture?

And, uh, the piano players mainly played classical music. Uh-huh. And, uh, the madams especially didn't care for, for, for, for, ragtime. Jazz, blues, ragtime. Sure. Yeah. And, uh, but blues never somehow filtered into the environment. I mean, they just didn't play the blues here. Uh, the city never produced any significant blues singers. Yeah. People like Lizzie Miles or, or Blue Lou weren't really blues singers, they were pop singers. Uh-huh. And Lizzie got famous for singing obscene lyrics. And, uh, the, uh, the only real blues singer that I knew was New Orleans' Willie Jackson.
Well, why do you think that is, that we didn't produce any blues?

Well, because it's not indigenous. You see, the thing is that the blues, uh, really belong to a different geographical area. Uh-huh. And, uh, this was a stomp town. I mean, you didn't have the kind of moaning and groaning and unhappiness in New Orleans as you had in the country. Uh-huh. And, uh, if you were from Clarksdale, Mississippi or something like that, then you were into the blues. Uh-huh. Another thing that people don't think about is the fact that in other areas of the country where slaves were, came in through other ports, they were all Protestant colonies. Right. And the Protestant colonies didn't even allow secular music at all. So they had to do religious music, which eventually developed gospel music, out of which the blues grew.
And the New Orleans music grew as a result of the amalgam of military music and the minstrels.
And, uh, and eventually, you know, became a whole different musical form. And they just didn't think in that form. Uh-huh. But most of the historians don't even think about that.

Well, it's most of them from other places. Yeah. Sure. Oh, shall remain nameless. Um, so you don't think, so you don't think when Louie was working those saloons at Liberty Perdido in that area, that he was, that he, that he wasn't playing a lot of blues?
No, he would play an occasional blues, I'm sure. Uh-huh.
But, uh. But the bulk of his repertoire.
Yeah, it would have been stomps.
Yeah. Uh-huh. That's a good thing.
